title: Ember Smoked Mullet Dip
summary: Florida fish-camp classic — smoked mullet folded into a creamy, lemony dip with crackers.
story: Smoked fish dip is Florida fish-camp food, and mullet is the traditional fish for it — oily enough to take smoke beautifully. Brine it, smoke it low, flake it, and fold it into cream cheese with lemon and hot sauce. Don't overmix: you want flakes, not paste.

items: ¼ cup brown sugar (for the brine)

steps.title: Brine
steps.body: Dissolve the salt and brown sugar in the cold water. Brine the fillets 2–4 hours in the fridge.

steps.title: Dry
steps.body: Rinse, pat dry, and air-dry 30 minutes so the smoke sticks.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 200°F over oak or alder, 2–3 hours, until the fish flakes easily and has good color.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Flake the fish, picking out any bones. Fold into the cream cheese, mayo, lemon, green onions, hot sauce, Old Bay, and pepper. Don't overmix — flakes, not paste.

steps.title: Chill and serve
steps.body: Chill at least 2 hours. Serve with crackers and lemon wedges.

proTips: No mullet? Smoked kingfish or mahi works — but mullet's the real Florida deal.
The dip is better the next day. Make it ahead if you can.

title: Faust's Ember Candied Brisket Jerky
summary: Thin-sliced brisket with a brown sugar–molasses glaze, smoked low until it snaps. Meat candy.
story: Candied jerky is having a moment — thin brisket, sweet glaze, crisp snap. The trick is the thin slice and the low temp: too thick and it's chewy, too hot and the sugar burns before it dries. Slice the flat partially frozen and you'll get clean ⅛-inch slices.

items: ½ tsp MSG (optional — it's the secret)

steps.title: Slice thin
steps.body: Partially freeze the flat for 1 hour, then slice against the grain, ⅛ inch thick. Thin is everything.

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Whisk everything else into a marinade. Coat the slices and refrigerate 12–24 hours.

steps.title: Smoke low
steps.body: Lay slices on wire racks, not touching. Smoke at 170–180°F for 4–6 hours, flipping once, until they bend and crack but don't break.

steps.title: Candy it
steps.body: In the last hour, brush with a little brown sugar dissolved in warm water for the candied shell.

steps.title: Cool and store
steps.body: Cool completely — they crisp as they cool. Airtight container, 2 weeks.

proTips: Too thick = chewy. Too hot = burnt sugar. Thin slices and low temp are the whole game.
Eye of round works too if brisket flat is pricey — but brisket's the real deal.

title: Smoked Beef Cheeks (Barbacoa)
summary: The most underrated cut on the cow: smoked like brisket, braised till it surrenders, shredded into juicy barbacoa.
story: Beef cheeks are the brisket point's shy cousin — all that marbled, hardworking muscle, none of the fame. They take smoke beautifully, then go into a covered pan with broth and onion until a probe slides in like warm butter. Shred them, toss with the juices, and you've got barbacoa that eats like the best pulled brisket you ever had. A little goes a long way: this is rich meat.

items: ¼ cup Ember House Rub (or your favorite beef rub)

steps.title: Trim hard
steps.body: Cut away all the silver skin and hard fat. There is a lot of it on cheeks — be aggressive. What looks like meat but shines silver will never render.

steps.title: Rub and rest
steps.body: Thin coat of mustard, then rub heavy on all sides. Rest 30–60 minutes at room temp while the pit comes to 275°F.

steps.title: Smoke to the bark
steps.body: Oak or hickory, 4–5 hours, until the bark is set dark and the internal temp is around 165°F. Don't wrap yet — the bark needs to be finished first.

steps.title: Braise it down
steps.body: Into a pan with the broth, onion, and bay. Seal tight with foil. Back on the pit at 275°F for 2–3 hours.

steps.title: Probe, don't clock
steps.body: Start checking at 200°F. Done when the probe slides in with almost no resistance — usually 200–205°F. If it still feels tight, give it more time.

steps.title: Rest, then shred
steps.body: Rest 30–45 minutes, still covered. Shred it all and toss with the strained braising juices. Serve piled up as-is, or as barbacoa tacos with diced onion, cilantro, and lime.

proTips.text: Silver skin on cheeks is thick and sneaky. If you leave it, you'll be picking chewy bits out of shredded meat. Trim like you mean it.
Cheeks are rich — richer than brisket. Four to five pounds raw feeds 6–8 easily. Plan tacos, not plates.

milestones.label: Bark set
milestones.hint: Dark crust, ~165°F internal. Then into the pan.

milestones.label: Shred
milestones.hint: Rest 30–45 min, shred, toss with juices.

title: Ember Southwest BBQ Sauce
summary: Chipotle smoke, lime brightness, and cumin warmth with the Ember butter finish. Kelly's Southwest answer in a jar.
story: Every region needs its sauce, and the Southwest was the hole in the lineup. Dried chipotles bring the smoke, fresh lime keeps it bright, cumin gives it that desert warmth — and the butter stirred in off the heat makes it pour like silk. Built for ribs, chicken, and anything coming off a hot grill.

items: 2 chipotles in adobo, minced, plus 1 Tbsp adobo sauce

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Put everything except the butter in a saucepan and whisk it smooth.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, then lower and cook 20 minutes, stirring now and then, until it coats a spoon.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Off the heat, stir in the butter until melted and silky. Cool, bottle, and refrigerate — keeps about 3 weeks.

title: Hatch Green Chile Smothered Chicken Thighs
summary: Smoked chicken thighs with crispy skin, smothered New Mexico-style in roasted Hatch green chile sauce.
story: This is the New Mexico plate: simple salt brine, a chile-cumin rub, and a proper green chile sauce made from roasted Hatch chiles, onion, garlic, and chicken stock. The thighs smoke to crispy-skinned and juicy, then get buried in sauce. Warm tortillas are not optional.

steps.title: Brine
steps.body: Dissolve the salt in the water and brine the thighs 2 hours (or overnight in the fridge). Rinse and pat very dry.

steps.title: Rub and smoke
steps.body: Coat the thighs in the rub. Smoke at 275°F about 90 minutes, until the skin is crisp and the thickest thigh reads 165°F.

steps.title: Make the sauce
steps.body: While the chicken smokes, saute the onion in the oil until soft, add the garlic, chiles, cumin, and oregano, then pour in the stock. Simmer 20 minutes.

steps.title: Smother
steps.body: Plate the thighs and ladle the hot green chile sauce over the top. Serve with warm tortillas.

title: Hatch Chile Verde Pulled Pork
summary: Pork butt smoked low, then braised in Hatch chile verde until it shreds — built for warm tortillas.
story: Chile verde is one of the great braises, and the smoker makes it better. The butt takes on oak smoke for hours first, then finishes swimming in roasted Hatch chiles, tomatillos, and onion until it surrenders. Shred it through the braising juices, hit it with lime and cilantro, and pile it into tortillas.

steps.title: Rub
steps.body: Coat the butt all over in the rub. Rest at room temp while the smoker comes up to 250°F.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke fat-side up at 250°F to about 165°F internal, 6-7 hours, until the bark is set and the color is deep.

steps.title: Braise
steps.body: Set the butt in a deep pan with the chiles, tomatillos, onion, garlic, and broth. Cover tight with foil and return to the smoker until probe-tender near 203°F.

steps.title: Shred
steps.body: Rest 1 hour, then shred and fold through the chile verde in the pan. Finish with lime juice and cilantro. Serve with warm tortillas.

title: Hatch-Lime Wings with Green Chile Salsa
summary: Smoked wings in a Hatch chile-lime dry rub, crisped hot and served with green chile salsa for dipping.
story: No buffalo sauce here — these wings go the Southwest way. A dry rub of Hatch chile powder, cumin, and lime zest, low smoke, then a blast of heat for crackling skin. The green chile salsa on the side is for dunking, and it will not last long.

items: 3 lbs chicken wings, patted very dry

steps.title: Rub
steps.body: Toss the dry wings thoroughly in the rub. The baking powder is the crisp-skin trick — don't skip it.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F about 90 minutes until cooked through and the skin is starting to tighten.

steps.title: Crisp
steps.body: Move to high direct heat (or under the broiler) a few minutes per side until the skin crackles.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Stir the salsa ingredients together. Serve the wings dry-rubbed with the green chile salsa for dipping.

title: Chamorro BBQ Chicken
summary: Guam's backyard classic: chicken marinated overnight in soy, vinegar, lemon, onion, and garlic, grilled hot and basted.
story: On Guam, barbecue means this marinade — soy sauce, vinegar, lemon, onion, garlic, black pepper. Every family has its version; the overnight soak is non-negotiable. Hot grill, constant turning, constant basting, until the skin chars at the edges and the inside stays juicy. Serve it with red rice if you're doing it right.

items: 4 lbs bone-in chicken thighs and legs

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Whisk the marinade ingredients, pour over the chicken, cover, and refrigerate overnight — at least 8 hours. This is the traditional way; don't shortcut it.

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Grill over medium-high heat, turning every few minutes and basting with the marinade, 30-40 minutes until the thickest piece reads 165°F.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes before serving. Red rice on the side if you're doing it right.

title: Argentine Asado with Chimichurri
summary: Salt-only beef over wood embers, the Argentine way — with a bright chimichurri to cut the richness.
story: Asado isn't a recipe, it's a ritual: beef, coarse salt, wood fire, patience. No rubs, no injections, no sauce on the meat — the flavor comes from the embers and the cut. Chimichurri on the side is the one allowance, and it's non-negotiable. Cook it slow over real wood embers and let the beef speak.

items: 4 lbs beef short ribs (tira de asado) and/or vacio (flap), cut thick

steps.title: Salt the beef
steps.body: Salt the beef generously on all sides at least 1 hour before cooking — up to overnight in the fridge.

steps.title: Build embers
steps.body: Burn hardwood down to glowing embers. You want steady medium heat, no flames licking the meat.

steps.title: Grill slow
steps.body: Grill the beef over the embers, turning occasionally, until deeply crusted outside and medium-rare to medium inside — about 2 hours for thick cuts. Patience is the technique.

steps.title: Chimichurri
steps.body: Whisk the chimichurri ingredients together and rest 20 minutes. Slice the beef, salt once more if needed, and serve with chimichurri on the side — never on top before slicing.

title: Brazilian Picanha (Churrasco)
summary: The queen of churrasco: picanha with its fat cap, coarse salt, hot fire, sliced thin off the skewer.
story: In Brazil, picanha is sacred — top sirloin cap with a thick layer of fat, seasoned with nothing but coarse rock salt. Skewered in a C, roasted over hot coals, and sliced thin right off the skewer so the fat bastes every bite. If your butcher doesn't know the cut, ask for top sirloin cap with the fat left on.

items: 1 whole picanha (top sirloin cap), 3-4 lbs, fat cap intact

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Cut the picanha with the grain into 3 thick steaks. Fold each into a C and skewer through both ends — or skewer the whole roast. Coat heavily in coarse rock salt.

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Grill over hot charcoal, turning the skewer, until the fat cap is crisp and golden and the interior is medium-rare, about 45-60 minutes for a whole roast.

steps.title: Slice
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes. Slice thin against the grain — right off the skewer at the table if you want the full churrascaria show.

title: Jamaican Jerk Chicken
summary: The real jerk marinade — scotch bonnet, allspice, thyme — smoked over pimento wood the way Boston Bay does it.
story: Real jerk is a marinade, not a dry rub: scotch bonnets for fire, allspice (pimento) for that warm clove-pepper depth, fresh thyme, green onion. Traditionally it smokes slow over pimento wood in a pit in Portland parish. Pimento wood is hard to find stateside — charcoal with allspice berries tossed on the coals gets you close.

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Blend the marinade ingredients into a thick paste. Coat the chicken thoroughly, cover, and refrigerate overnight — 12 hours minimum for real jerk flavor.

steps.title: Smoke-grill
steps.body: Grill over medium charcoal with a handful of allspice berries (or pimento wood chunks) for smoke. Cook with the lid on, turning occasionally, 60-90 minutes to 165°F internal with charred edges.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes. Serve with lime wedges — and warn people about the heat.

title: Filipino Lechon Belly Roll
summary: Pork belly rolled with lemongrass and garlic, roasted to crackling — the fiesta centerpiece of the Philippines.
story: Lechon is the Philippines' celebration food — whole pig on a spit for fiestas. The belly roll is the home-cook version: same crackling skin, same juicy spiral, stuffed with lemongrass and garlic the way it's done back home. Salt the skin hard, dry it overnight, and don't open the lid to peek.

items: 1 pork belly slab, about 5 lbs, skin on

steps.title: Stuff and roll
steps.body: Butterfly the belly to even thickness. Season the meat side, lay in the lemongrass, garlic, and onion, roll tight, and tie with butcher's twine every 2 inches.

steps.title: Dry the skin
steps.body: Salt the skin heavily and refrigerate uncovered overnight. Dry skin is crackling skin — don't skip this.

steps.title: Roast
steps.body: Roast at 325°F about 3-4 hours to 195°F internal, until the skin is deep golden and shatters when tapped.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Rest 20 minutes, slice thick, and serve with the spiced vinegar for dipping.
